parts.title: Tennis coaching for a child
parts.context: A mother asks about tennis coaching for her daughter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a mother phoning a tennis club to ask about coaching for her daughter. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Westfield Tennis Club, Ben speaking.

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: Hello. I'm calling about tennis coaching for my daughter. She's been asking me for weeks.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Lovely. I'll take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The coaching is for the caller's daughter, so 'daughter' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: Sophie Hughes. That's H-U-G-H-E-S.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Hughes. And your daughter's name?

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: Ellie. That's E-L-L-I-E.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: How old is she?

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: She's eleven.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Has she played before?

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: She's played at school for two years, but only in games lessons, so she's had no proper coaching.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Which day would suit you best?

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: Saturdays, I think. During the week she has too much homework.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: We run three kinds of coaching. The Starters group is on Saturdays at nine, with up to six children, which means every child gets plenty of attention. It costs thirty-six pounds a month.

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: That sounds perfect. What about the other groups?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: The Intermediate group is for children who can already rally. It starts at ten on Saturdays, with up to eight children, and it costs forty-eight pounds a month.

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: I think Starters is right for Ellie. Do you also give private lessons?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Yes, if she wants some extra practice. A private lesson costs thirty pounds an hour, and the times are arranged with the coach.

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: Does she need her own racket?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Not at first. We have rackets for hire at two pounds a session, and you can buy one when you're sure she'll carry on.

script.speaker: sophie
script.text: That's very helpful. Can we try a session first?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Yes, the first one is free. Just turn up at nine on Saturday, in sports shoes. Tennis shoes aren't necessary, but trainers with a flat sole are best.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A school sports day
parts.context: A head teacher briefs parent helpers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a head teacher briefing parent helpers before a school sports day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for volunteering to help on sports day. I'm Mrs Nolan, the head teacher. I'll explain how the day will work.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Sports day will be on Thursday of next week. We usually hold it on a Friday, but the field is booked for a football match, so we've had to change it.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: The first race will start at half past nine, and we'll finish by lunchtime. Parents who aren't helping are welcome to watch, and we'll put out chairs along the side of the field.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: If it rains, I'm afraid we won't move indoors, because the hall isn't big enough. The whole event will be postponed to the following week.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Please don't park in the school car park, which is needed for the equipment lorry. Use the church hall car park, which is five minutes' walk away, and I'm grateful to the vicar for allowing it.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Children should bring a water bottle and a sun hat. They'll wear their normal PE kit, and we'll provide fruit and a drink at the end.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Now let me describe the events and the age groups. The youngest children, in Year One, take part in the egg-and-spoon race. It's the most popular race, and I'm afraid the eggs are usually the first casualty.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Year Two have the sack race, which is chaotic and very funny. Year Three do an obstacle course, which isn't on your list because it's supervised by the teachers.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: Year Four run the relay, in teams of four, and it's important that the batons are handed over properly, so we need two adults at each changeover. Year Five do the long jump, and we need someone to measure and record the results.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: And Year Six finish the morning with the tug of war, which has been a tradition for forty years. The teachers will take on the Year Six team, and I'm told the teachers have a secret weapon this year.

script.speaker: nolan
script.text: If you could all collect your coloured badges from the office, you'll see the station you've been given. Thank you again for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A composting scheme
parts.context: Two students plan a composting scheme for their university.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Rosa and Amos, planning a composting scheme at their university. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Amos, shall we go through the proposal for the composting scheme? Dr Lim wants it by the end of the week.

script.speaker: amos
script.text: Yes. The aim is to reduce the amount of food waste that goes to landfill, where it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: And how much waste does the canteen produce? I've got the figure here somewhere.

script.speaker: amos
script.text: About five hundred kilograms a week, and about a third of that is food that could be composted.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Where shall we put the compost bins? Our first idea was next to the library.

script.speaker: amos
script.text: But that's too far from the canteen, and the smell would annoy the students. Behind the canteen is better, because the kitchen staff can reach it easily.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: We ran a trial for two weeks. What went wrong?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: The main problem was that students put the wrong things in the bins, plastic forks and packaging, mostly. The smell wasn't a problem, and we didn't see any rats.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: How do we deal with that?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: Signs with pictures, I think, showing what goes in and what doesn't. A fine would be silly, and we can't ask staff to supervise the bins all day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Now, in the guide for students, we need to explain what can go into the compost. Coffee grounds first.

script.speaker: amos
script.text: They're good. They add nitrogen, which balances the dry material, and the cafés give us plenty.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Meat?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: Better kept out of a small heap, because it attracts pests like rats and flies.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Paper cups?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: They look harmless, but most have a thin plastic lining, so they must stay out.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Garden waste, like branches and woody stems?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: That's fine, but it takes the longest to break down, so it needs to be cut up small.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: And eggshells?

script.speaker: amos
script.text: They're fine, but they need to be crushed first, or they stay in the compost for months.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Good. I'll draw the poster this weekend.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of vaccination
parts.context: A medical history lecture on vaccines.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of vaccination. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Vaccination is one of the most successful medical developments in history. Today I'd like to trace its story, from a single experiment to a global programme.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Before vaccines, smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases. About one in three of the people who caught it died, and many survivors were left blind or scarred for life.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In seventeen ninety-six, an English doctor named Edward Jenner noticed something odd. Milkmaids, who often caught a mild disease called cowpox from the cows, seemed never to catch smallpox. Jenner guessed that cowpox gave some kind of protection.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: He tested the idea on a young boy, giving him a small amount of material from a cowpox sore. Later, he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy stayed healthy. The word vaccine itself comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the nineteenth century, the French scientist Louis Pasteur developed the idea. He made vaccines for animal diseases, such as anthrax, and for a terrible human disease, rabies, by weakening the germs that cause them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the nineteen fifties, an American researcher named Jonas Salk produced the first successful vaccine for polio, which had been paralysing thousands of children every summer.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A vaccine protects the people who receive it, and it also protects others. If enough people are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily, and even those who are not protected are safe. This is known as herd immunity.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The greatest triumph was the campaign against smallpox. After a worldwide programme, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in nineteen eighty, the only human disease to have been wiped out.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today, vaccines still save millions of lives. But one challenge is that false information spreads very easily, especially online, and some people have become afraid of vaccination without good reason. Next week we'll look at antibiotics.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
